overview: Pakistan became independent in 1947, emerging from the end of British rule in South Asia. The atlas begins this label in 1945, two years too early. Its snapshots are broad map coverage, not exact borders or a claim that every part shared one political history.

periods.title: Before independence
periods.summary: The imported start precedes the creation of Pakistan in 1947. Read this short map interval as late colonial context.

periods.title: A new dominion
periods.summary: Independence brought a constituent assembly; Pakistan initially remained a dominion while a constitution was debated.

periods.title: Republic and military intervention
periods.summary: The 1956 republic was followed by the 1958 military takeover. The geographically separated eastern and western wings remained deeply divided.

periods.title: Bangladesh becomes independent
periods.summary: War and mass displacement ended the two-wing state; Bangladesh emerged as a separate country in 1971.

periods.title: Constitution and interrupted civilian rule
periods.summary: The 1973 constitutional framework survived repeated alteration and military interventions, including the takeover of 1999.

periods.title: Civilian institutions and continuing pressures
periods.summary: Military rule ended in 2008. An electoral transfer followed in 2013; later elections and civil liberties remained contested in dated reporting.

sections.title: Independence, government and a changing map

items.text: Partition in 1947 uprooted families on an enormous scale. Muslim refugees moved toward Pakistan while many Hindus and Sikhs fled toward India; communal violence tore families apart. Independence was both the making of new countries and an immense human emergency.

Pakistan became an Islamic republic on 23 March 1956. The constitution introduced in 1973 established a parliamentary system with a prime minister, a president and two legislative chambers: the National Assembly and Senate. These institutions changed how authority was organized, even when their operation was interrupted.

The Awami League won a majority in the 1970 national election, but the transfer of power broke down. In March 1971 the army launched a crackdown in the eastern wing. Civilians faced mass killings and flight, while Bengali resistance developed into a struggle for independence.

The 1971 war ended with an independent Bangladesh. The atlas nevertheless keeps the eastern wing inside its Pakistan feature for the entire 1960 to 1994 interval. That outline is wrong after 1971. It must not be read as Pakistan continuing to govern Bangladesh.

The army seized power in 1958, 1977 and 1999. The last of those periods of direct military rule ended in 2008. Civilian elections therefore belong to a history of repeated interruptions, rather than an uninterrupted democratic sequence.

Pakistan conducted underground nuclear tests on 28 May 1998. The next day the UN Security Council condemned them and called for restraint. This development made regional diplomacy and the danger of escalation especially consequential for ordinary families on both sides of the India-Pakistan border.

Kashmir remains disputed. The map’s northern outlines represent an imported cartographic choice, not a ruling on sovereignty. Pakistan’s state history and the experiences of people in disputed territories require more care than a single coloured polygon can provide.

sections.title: Work, art, calendars and family meals

items.text: A cargo truck can also be a travelling art gallery. Smithsonian’s 2002 example combined carved wooden doors associated with Swat and Peshawar, Sindh-style inlay and peacock designs familiar in Punjab and Sindh. These were skilled workshop traditions, with regional differences visible on a working vehicle.

The same Smithsonian account describes decorated truck interiors with mirrors, beads and fancy cushions, and owners competing over elaborate designs. Karachi’s painters and repair workshops brought styles together as drivers collected goods at the port. Even a delivery job could arrive dressed for a parade.

Sialkot’s football industry also exposed a difficult contrast: some children stitched balls instead of enjoying childhood. An ILO project whose first phase ran from 1997 to 1999 aimed to remove children from stitching while providing social protection and strengthening local institutions. An announced project was a beginning, not proof that every problem had disappeared.

Among Kalasha communities in the Hindu Kush, Suri Jagek means observing the sun. People relate the sun, moon, stars and shadows to their mountain surroundings to organize farming and a calendar of gatherings and ceremonies. Stories, songs and proverbs help pass this knowledge on. This is a particular community’s tradition, not a custom shared by all Pakistanis.

At a 2024 nutrition session in Lyari, Karachi, Seema and her young son Ayan encountered four versions of khichri: soft rice and lentils served plain or with carrot, squash or potato. Demonstrators chose foods families could afford locally. The lesson was practical: one familiar pot could produce several different lunches.

Those cooking sessions also discussed handwashing before and after food preparation. Seema, a mother of four, later told other pregnant women and parents what she had learned. Family care could spread through neighbourly conversation as well as through clinics, while the cost of ingredients still constrained what households could serve.

Pakistan established its Lady Health Workers programme in 1994. WHO describes women bringing primary-health and family-planning services closer to communities, with later training in childhood illness. Community activities focused on problems such as diarrhoea and pneumonia. A health system could reach a family at home, rather than requiring every first conversation to happen in a distant hospital.

In UNICEF’s March 2024 account, twelve-year-old Farzana lived in Musa Jasser village in Sindh. Long journeys to collect water with her mother had kept her away from school. A nearby hand pump, set on a raised platform for protection against flooding, changed the family’s daily timetable.

With water much closer to home, Farzana returned to school, where she studied Sindhi, Urdu and English. She also had time to play football with friends. A water pump’s achievement can be counted in lessons and games as well as buckets: less time carrying water gave a child more choices.

At Hashimabad Jamrud Government High School, UNICEF reported new water facilities in May 2021: four solar-powered water chillers and three handwashing stations with soap. The headteacher also described running hot and cold water in the washrooms. Toilets and taps were part of keeping a school usable during the pandemic, not glamorous extras.

Schoolwork during lockdown could not simply move onto a phone. Fifteen-year-old Mushahid lacked a device for his school’s WhatsApp group. His headteacher arranged assignments for students without access, and teachers later checked their work. This small workaround shows how unequal access shaped a very ordinary problem: getting tomorrow’s homework.

A January 2026 UNICEF report describes girls in Karachi using tablets for mathematics, science and social studies through the Sindh Learning Passport. They replayed difficult lessons and helped one another. Their practical request was headphones: a room full of lesson videos could get rather loud. These were specific classrooms, not universal access across the country.

Malala Yousafzai’s Urdu diary, published by the BBC in 2009, described life under Taliban control in Swat and defended schooling. She survived an attack in 2012 and received a share of the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize for children’s right to education. Her story links writing, danger and determined advocacy for girls’ learning.

sections.title: Science and words on everyday objects

items.text: Abdus Salam shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics with Sheldon Glashow and Steven Weinberg. Their work connected the weak and electromagnetic interactions within a common theory. The achievement was a way of explaining the behaviour of elementary particles, part of an international scientific effort rather than a machine invented by one country.

Salam returned to teach in Lahore in 1951, but research isolation eventually took him abroad. At the international physics centre he created in Trieste, Italy, visiting associates could work with other researchers and then return to teach in their home countries. Building connections between scientists was one answer to the problem of working far from major research centres.

An early banknote provides a short Urdu writing sample: حکومت پاکستان, transliterated Hukūmat-e Pākistān, means “Government of Pakistan.” The State Bank transcribes it on modified Indian notes authorized under the 1947 monetary order, alongside the English wording. This is a documented early-independence inscription, reproduced here in modern type rather than as a facsimile.

Money also recorded the country’s linguistic geography. The State Bank’s first two-rupee series, issued on 1 March 1949, carried English, Urdu and Bengali. A small piece of paper thus addressed readers across the two wings of Pakistan. Its crescent watermark was another feature described in the bank’s account.

ending.text: Pakistan continues as a state; Bangladesh’s independence in 1971 was a territorial and political break, not Pakistan’s disappearance. Constitutional government has endured alongside military influence and contested elections. The political assessment here is dated to September 2024; later school and family reports describe particular communities through January 2026, not a comprehensive account of every current condition.
